controls.label: Color + brightness
controls.qualification: The star's color, darker where TESS saw it dimmer (contrast drawn stronger) · March and April 2022, mapped in this project
controls.notes: GJ 504 in its own color, darker where its light in TESS's images of March and April 2022 says it was darker. As the star turned once in 3.44 days its light rose and fell by 0.54%. The contrast is drawn far stronger than it is, so the eye can see it: the darkest part gives 34.3% less light than the brightest, and is drawn as a much darker tone of the star's own hue; the Brightness map's scale has the measured values. The longitudes of the darker and brighter parts are measured. Their latitudes and shapes are not: they are the smoothest that reproduce the light. No change of color is drawn, because none is measured. Spots come and go within weeks or months: this is the star then. The darkening toward the edge is the Color dataset's limb law, drawn 1.5 times as strong.

controls.label: Brightness map
controls.qualification: Mapped in this project · TESS mission light curve, sector 23
controls.notes: Where the star's surface was darker and brighter in TESS sector 23, worked out in this project from how its light rose and fell by 0.54% as it turned once in 3.44 days. The light curve is the mission's own; the criteria of Holcomb et al. (2022, ApJ 936, 138) decide that it shows the star turning, and starry finds the map that reproduces it. The longitudes of the dark and bright regions are fixed by the data; their latitudes are not. The map is made at the tilt the page draws the star with, 19°. Step through the 2 maps to see the spots change.
controls.legendNote: Darker: dimmer than the star's mean surface; white: brighter. Black line: 19° S; the star never shows us what lies below it.

controls.label: Color
controls.qualification: Color of a blackbody at the star's published temperature. The disc itself is unresolved.
controls.notes: The color of a 6,200 K blackbody, the star's published temperature; Gaia DR3 has no sampled spectrum of a star this bright. No image of its surface exists, and no darkening toward the edge is drawn.

controls.label: Radial field
controls.qualification: Mapped in this project · CFHT ESPaDOnS spectra, Apr 2025
controls.notes: The star's large-scale magnetic field in Apr 2025, reconstructed in this project from 19 archived ESPaDOnS spectra with the published codes LSDpy and ZDIpy. It is this project's reduction, not a published map.
controls.legendNote: Red: field pointing out of the star; blue: into it. Black line: 19° S; the star never shows us what lies below it.

controls.label: Derived corona
controls.notes: No telescope has imaged this corona, and this is not a published result: it is derived here from the star's magnetic map by a standard method. Gas at rest is placed along the line where the field of the Apr 2025 map reverses, and the wind everywhere else. How much gas there is follows from three numbers. The star's X-ray output is measured (Freund et al. (2022), A&A 664, A105). Its coronal temperature, 5.5 million kelvin, is not measured: it is the temperature stars of this X-ray output have (Johnstone & Güdel (2015), A&A 578, A129). Its mass loss, 63 times the Sun's, is not measured either: it is what the X-ray output suggests (Wood et al. (2021), ApJ 915, 37). Stars with a measured wind lie within a factor of 5 of that relation, and one is 38 times below it. Drawn out to 4 stellar radii in the star's own color; at each distance brightness is proportional to density.

physical.credit: Published or catalogue radius at the Gaia distance; Gaia DR3 astrometry; no measured rotation axis (display convention)
